nodes.label: Fundamental Identities and Simplifying Trigonometric Expressions
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background from Trigonometric Functions (radian measure, unit-circle and general-angle definitions of all six trigonometric functions, quadrant signs, even/odd symmetries, cofunctions, and sin² θ + cos² θ = 1) and from Polynomials and Factoring (distributing, GCF factoring, difference of squares, quadratic trinomial factoring, and combining rational expressions). Organizes the fundamental identity toolkit—reciprocal, quotient, even/odd, cofunction (written in radians such as sin(π/2 − x) = cos x), and all three Pythagorean identities, explicitly deriving 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = csc² x by dividing sin² x + cos² x = 1 by cos² x and sin² x on their valid domains. Trains recognizing rearranged forms (such as 1 − cos² x = sin² x and sec² x − 1 = tan² x) and simplifying trigonometric expressions using algebraic moves: factoring out common trigonometric factors, factoring differences of squares like cos⁴ x − sin⁴ x, forming common denominators, converting expressions into sine and cosine, and noting excluded values where denominators vanish. Explicitly warns against illegal algebra such as distributing squares across sums (sin x + cos x)² ≠ sin² x + cos² x or canceling terms across addition. Enables the learner to rewrite and simplify complex trigonometric expressions into compact equivalent forms while tracking domain validity. Leaves formal identity proof strategies, compound-angle formulas, and equation solving to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Inverse Trigonometric Functions: Domains, Ranges, and Graphs
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background from Trigonometric Functions (graphs, periodicity, asymptotes, and exact special-angle values of sin, cos, and tan in radians) and basic function concepts (one-to-one functions, the horizontal line test, and reflecting a graph across y = x to form an inverse). Explains why periodic trigonometric functions have no global inverse on ℝ and constructs the standard principal-value domain restrictions that yield arcsin x (sin⁻¹ x, domain [−1, 1], range [−π/2, π/2]), arccos x (cos⁻¹ x, domain [−1, 1], range [0, π]), and arctan x (tan⁻¹ x, domain ℝ, range (−π/2, π/2) with horizontal asymptotes y = ±π/2). Emphasizes the critical notation warning that sin⁻¹ x denotes the inverse function, never the reciprocal 1/sin x = csc x, and graphs each inverse function by reflecting the restricted branch across y = x. Trains exact evaluation at special ratios—especially negative inputs where range choices diverge sharply (e.g., arcsin(−½) = −π/6 and arctan(−1) = −π/4 in Quadrant IV, versus arccos(−½) = 2π/3 in Quadrant II)—and explains how arccot, arcsec, and arccsc are evaluated via reciprocals while noting standard principal-range conventions. Enables the learner to state domains, ranges, and graphs of the inverse trigonometric functions and evaluate exact principal values reliably. Leaves nested compositions and equation solving to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Proving and Disproving Trigonometric Identities
nodes.explanation: Builds on fundamental identities and algebraic simplification to develop disciplined proof techniques for verifying trigonometric identities—contrasting an identity (true for all x in the common domain) with a conditional equation (true only for particular solutions). Establishes the core logical rule of identity verification: never assume the target equality by performing non-reversible operations across the equals sign (such as squaring both sides or multiplying across); instead transform one side (usually the more complex side) into the other through a valid chain of equalities, or transform both sides independently to the same expression and verify reversibility. Develops a strategic verification toolkit: multiplying numerator and denominator by conjugates such as 1 ± sin x or sec x ± tan x to trigger Pythagorean substitutions, combining or splitting fractions, factoring trigonometric polynomials, and reducing stubborn expressions to sines and cosines. Also trains disproving false candidate identities by exhibiting a single concrete angle in the common domain where the two sides disagree (warning that checking one or two angles can never prove an identity). Enables the learner to construct clean, logically sound proofs of trigonometric identities and refute invalid ones, leaving compound-angle identities to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Sum and Difference Identities for Cosine, Sine, and Tangent
nodes.explanation: Builds on fundamental identities and identity-verification discipline (and uses unit-circle coordinates and the distance formula from prerequisite geometry/trigonometry) to derive and apply the angle-addition and angle-subtraction identities. Proves cos(α − β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β geometrically by equating the chord length between unit-circle points (cos α, sin α) and (cos β, sin β) to the congruent rotated chord between (cos(α − β), sin(α − β)) and (1, 0), explicitly refuting the linearity fallacy cos(α − β) ≠ cos α − cos β. Derives cos(α + β) via even/odd symmetry (replacing β with −β), derives sin(α ± β) via the cofunction bridge sin θ = cos(π/2 − θ), and derives tan(α ± β) = (tan α ± tan β)/(1 ∓ tan α tan β) by dividing sin(α ± β) by cos(α ± β) and dividing numerator and denominator by cos α cos β. Trains four core uses: computing exact values at non-standard angles such as 15°, 75°, and 5π/12; evaluating sin(α ± β), cos(α ± β), and tan(α ± β) when only one ratio and quadrant of α and β are known; collapsing expanded forms back into a single function; and verifying identities such as reduction formulas (sin(π − x), cos(x + π/2)) and tangent shifts. Leaves double-angle, half-angle, product-to-sum, and auxiliary-angle formulas to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Double-Angle, Power-Reducing, and Half-Angle Identities
nodes.explanation: Builds on the sum and difference identities to derive and apply the double-angle, power-reducing, and half-angle identity families. Sets β = α in the sum formulas to prove sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ, cos 2θ = cos² θ − sin² θ = 2 cos² θ − 1 = 1 − 2 sin² θ (highlighting when each of the three cosine forms is strategically best), and tan 2θ = (2 tan θ)/(1 − tan² θ), warning against the common error sin 2θ ≠ 2 sin θ. Rearranges the two single-function forms of cos 2θ to derive the power-reducing identities sin² θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, cos² θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2, and tan² θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ), practicing degree reduction of higher powers such as sin⁴ x or sin² x cos² x into first-power cosines (a key bridge to calculus integration). Substitutes θ = α/2 into the power-reducing formulas to establish the half-angle identities for sin(α/2), cos(α/2), and tan(α/2) (including the sign-free rational forms tan(α/2) = (1 − cos α)/sin α = sin α / (1 + cos α)), emphasizing the essential quadrant bridge: dividing the quadrant inequality for α by 2 determines the quadrant of α/2 and hence the correct ± sign. Enables the learner to compute exact double- and half-angle values from quadrant data, reduce trig powers, and prove multi-angle identities, leaving equation solving to the equation branch.

nodes.label: Product-to-Sum and Sum-to-Product Identities
nodes.explanation: Builds on the sum and difference identities to convert back and forth between products and sums/differences of sines and cosines. Derives the four product-to-sum identities (for sin α cos β, cos α sin β, cos α cos β, and sin α sin β) directly by adding or subtracting the expansion pairs for sin(α ± β) and cos(α ± β). Introduces the linear substitution bridge u = α + β, v = α − β (so α = (u + v)/2 and β = (u − v)/2) to invert those relations into the four sum-to-product identities (for sin u ± sin v and cos u ± cos v), keeping track of the crucial negative sign in cos u − cos v = −2 sin((u + v)/2) sin((u − v)/2). Trains using product-to-sum to compute exact values like sin(75°) cos(15°) and simplify trigonometric products, and using sum-to-product to factor sums such as sin 5x + sin x into products (directly preparing for multi-angle equation solving) and prove quotient identities like (sin 3x − sin x)/(cos 3x + cos x) = tan x, noting the physical interpretation of cos u + cos v as a carrier wave modulated by a slower beat envelope. Enables the learner to transform between additive and multiplicative trigonometric forms accurately.

nodes.label: Compositions of Trigonometric and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes inverse trigonometric functions and fundamental trigonometric identities to evaluate and simplify nested compositions in both orders. First contrasts the safe cancellation f(f⁻¹(u)) = u (valid whenever u lies in the domain of f⁻¹) with the hazardous reverse order f⁻¹(f(x)), which equals x ONLY when x lies in the principal range of f⁻¹; trains the essential two-step reduction when x lies outside the principal range (evaluate f(x) or its quadrant sign and reference angle, then pick the unique angle in the principal range of f⁻¹ matching that value, e.g., arcsin(sin(5π/6)) = π/6 and arccos(cos(−π/3)) = π/3). Second, develops mixed compositions g(f⁻¹(u))—such as tan(arccos(−3/5)), sec(arctan u), and sin(arccos u)—by setting θ = f⁻¹(u), identifying the quadrant of θ from the principal range of f⁻¹ (so signs are guaranteed exact for both positive and negative u), and constructing a labeled reference right triangle or applying a Pythagorean identity to obtain exact numeric values or algebraic expressions (noting domain conditions such as |u| ≤ 1 for √(1 − u²)). Enables the learner to evaluate nested trig/inverse-trig expressions without falling into cancellation traps and convert inverse-trig compositions into algebraic form.

nodes.label: Compound-Angle Identities with Inverse Trigonometric Functions
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing inverse-trig compositions with sum, difference, and double-angle identities to evaluate and prove identities combining multiple inverse trigonometric expressions. Trains setting α = f⁻¹(u) and β = g⁻¹(v) with explicit quadrant tracking, applying sin(α ± β), cos(α ± β), tan(α ± β), or sin(2α)/cos(2α) together with reference triangles to find exact values and algebraic formulas for expressions such as cos(arcsin u + arccos v), sin(2 arctan x), and tan(arccos(3/5) − arcsin(−5/13)). Develops proofs of classical inverse-trig relations including arcsin x + arccos x = π/2 (for |x| ≤ 1) and arctan(1/2) + arctan(1/3) = π/4, emphasizing the essential range check: showing tan(α + β) = 1 proves α + β = π/4 only after bounding α + β inside (−π/2, π/2) so a π-shift cannot hide. Enables the learner to manipulate composite inverse-trig identities with full quadrant rigor.

nodes.label: Basic Trigonometric Equations and General Solutions
nodes.explanation: Builds on inverse trigonometric functions (and uses unit-circle symmetry and periodicity from Trigonometric Functions) to solve basic conditional equations sin x = c, cos x = c, tan x = c, and their reciprocal forms csc x = c, sec x = c, cot x = c. Establishes existence criteria immediately (|c| ≤ 1 for sin and cos; |c| ≥ 1 for csc and sec; all c ∈ ℝ for tan and cot) and develops the complete solution-finding bridge connecting one principal value from arcsin/arccos/arctan to ALL solutions: on one fundamental period [0, 2π), sine yields θ₀ and π − θ₀ (adjusted into [0, 2π)), cosine yields θ₀ and 2π − θ₀, and tangent yields θ₀ and θ₀ + π; across all of ℝ, adding integer multiples of the period gives the general solution families (x = θ₀ + 2πk or π − θ₀ + 2πk for sine; x = ±θ₀ + 2πk for cosine; x = θ₀ + πk for tangent, k ∈ ℤ). Covers both exact special-value equations (such as cos x = −√3/2) and non-special equations expressed exactly with inverse functions (such as sin x = 0.4 yielding arcsin(0.4) + 2πk and π − arcsin(0.4) + 2πk) or rounded numerically. Explicitly addresses the common mistake of reporting only the single calculator inverse value and missing the second quadrant family. Enables the learner to find complete bounded-interval and general solutions for any single-function equation of argument x.

nodes.label: Multiple-Angle and Shifted-Argument Trigonometric Equations
nodes.explanation: Builds on basic trigonometric equations to solve linear-argument equations of the form f(kx + φ) = c (with rational k ≠ 0 and phase shift φ, such as sin(3x) = √2/2, cos(2x − π/3) = −½, or tan(x/2) = √3) on both ℝ and bounded intervals such as [0, 2π). Develops the essential substitution bridge u = kx + φ: first write the complete general solution for u (including the +2πk or +πk periodic family), then divide by k and shift to solve for x before generating all integer values of k that place x in the target interval—or equivalently rescale the target interval [a, b) to [ka + φ, kb + φ) before finding u. Directly diagnoses and eliminates the single most common error in multiple-angle solving: finding solutions for u only in [0, 2π) and dividing by k, which silently drops (k − 1) periods of valid solutions. Applies this method to answer real-world sinusoidal inverse questions left open in Trigonometric Functions (finding all times t in a cycle when a periodic model reaches a specified intermediate height or temperature). Enables the learner to capture every valid solution of multiple-angle and phase-shifted trigonometric equations without omissions.

nodes.label: Factoring, Quadratic-Type, and Pythagorean-Substitution Equations
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes fundamental trigonometric identities (and prior polynomial factoring/quadratic formula background) with basic trigonometric equation solving to solve nonlinear equations in a single angle x. Trains four algebraic reduction strategies: (1) moving all terms to one side and factoring out a common trigonometric factor (such as sin x cos x = sin x), strongly refuting the fatal error of dividing both sides by sin x and losing all solutions of sin x = 0; (2) solving quadratic-type equations via substitution u = f(x) (factoring trinomials like 2 cos² x − cos x − 1 = 0, applying the quadratic formula with inverse trig when non-factorable, and discarding roots outside [−1, 1] for sin/cos); (3) converting mixed-function equations into one function using Pythagorean or reciprocal identities (such as 2 sin² x + 3 cos x = 3 or sec² x − 2 tan x = 4); and (4) squaring both sides when linear mixtures like sin x + cos x = 1 resist direct substitution, with mandatory substitution checks back into the original equation to reject extraneous roots and domain-excluded values (such as points where tan x or sec x is undefined). Enables the learner to reduce and solve algebraic and quadratic-type trigonometric equations completely without losing valid roots or admitting extraneous ones.

nodes.label: Harmonic Combinations a sin x + b cos x and the Auxiliary-Angle Method
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes sum and difference identities with multiple-angle/shifted-argument equation solving to collapse any same-frequency linear combination a sin x + b cos x (with a, b not both zero) into a single shifted sinusoid R sin(x + φ) (or R cos(x − ψ)). Derives the auxiliary-angle bridge by factoring out R = √(a² + b²) so the unit vector (a/R, b/R) satisfies (a/R)² + (b/R)² = 1, ensuring a unique angle φ ∈ [0, 2π) with cos φ = a/R and sin φ = b/R so that a sin x + b cos x = R(sin x cos φ + cos x sin φ) = R sin(x + φ). Explicitly addresses the quadrant pitfall: φ = arctan(b/a) works only when a > 0, whereas a < 0 requires adding π so φ matches the exact signs of (a/R, b/R). Applies this single-sinusoid representation to read exact amplitude R, phase shift, and maximum/minimum values immediately, and to solve equations a sin x + b cos x = c cleanly as sin(x + φ) = c/R (identifying no-solution cases |c| > R instantly and avoiding the extraneous-root hazard of squaring both sides). Enables the learner to combine same-frequency sinusoids and solve linear harmonic equations exactly.

nodes.label: Solving Multi-Angle and Sum-to-Product Trigonometric Equations
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes double-angle/half-angle identities, sum-to-product identities, multiple-angle solving, and factoring/quadratic trigonometric equations to solve general equations involving mixed angles or multiple frequencies. Trains strategic identity selection rather than blind rewriting: replacing cos 2x with 1 − 2 sin² x in cos 2x + sin x = 0 (or 2 cos² x − 1 in cos 2x = cos x) to produce a single-function quadratic; using sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x to factor equations like sin 2x − cos x = 0; applying sum-to-product to factor mixed-frequency equations such as sin 5x + sin x = 0 or cos 3x − cos x = 0 directly into products of multiple-angle factors (each solved via the multiple-angle method); and handling half-angle or tangent-cotangent equations while checking domain exclusions and extraneous roots when squaring or rationalizing. Emphasizes uniting solution families cleanly without duplicating or omitting roots on [0, 2π) or ℝ. Enables the learner to choose an effective identity transformation and obtain complete, verified solution sets for advanced trigonometric equations.

nodes.label: Trigonometric Inequalities on the Unit Circle and Graphs
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing multiple-angle and algebraic/quadratic trigonometric equation solving (together with unit-circle coordinates and sinusoidal graphs from Trigonometric Functions) to solve inequalities such as sin x > ½, cos(2x) ≤ −√3/2, tan x < 1, and 2 sin² x − sin x > 0 on [0, 2π) and on all of ℝ. Develops the boundary-and-test-arc method: first solve the associated equality to locate exact boundary angles (and vertical asymptotes for tangent/cotangent), then shade valid arcs directly on the unit circle or intervals on a one-period graph to read exact open/closed interval unions (handling wrap-around across 0 / 2π cleanly and writing periodic interval families [a + 2πk, b + 2πk]). Explicitly warns against sign-flip errors when multiplying by variable trigonometric factors and against crossing vertical asymptotes of tan x. Enables the learner to express exact solution sets of basic, multiple-angle, and factored trigonometric inequalities in interval notation.
